1: Chapter 1: A Guest on a Rainy Night
It had been raining in Felsheim for three days. In the spring, Anna Weber's older sister had gone to Berlin, and since then Anna had been running the village's little pharmacy on her own.
At nightfall she closed the shutters, counted the day's takings, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had barely lain down when there was a fierce pounding at the door downstairs. A man's voice called out, "Is anyone there?"
At the door stood a young man, soaked to the skin, his left arm wrapped in a bloodied cloth. He introduced himself as Konrad Wolf and said he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
"I need a bandage," Wolf said quietly. "I can pay. Would thirty-five hundred marks be enough?"
He pulled a letter wrapped in oilskin from his jacket. "This letter must reach Steinbach Monastery before the eighteenth of May."
Anna must have been blind — only now did she notice how pale he was.
Even so, she refused his money and said only, "Tomorrow morning I'll take you into the mountains."
2: They set off at daybreak. Anna carried a basket on her back with bread, healing herbs, and an old umbrella in it.

Halfway up, they came across old Hans Becker, who was chopping wood. He set his axe aside and said quietly that three strangers had been asking at the village entrance the evening before about an injured young man.
"Take the path, Anna," said Hans Becker. "The main road isn't safe." Anna thanked him.
The path was narrow and slippery. Anna went ahead, placing each step with care. Wolf followed her in silence.
Around midday the rain stopped, the fog slowly lifted, and in the distance the roof of Steinbach Abbey came into view. At the gate stood a nun, Sister Hildegard, who received the abbey's guests.
Sister Hildegard took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. "The abbess has been waiting 2 years for this letter."
Wolf said to Anna, "I owe you my life." Anna smiled. "Then next time, you can fix the roof of my apothecary shop." Wolf stayed at the abbey.
In the evening, Anna made her way down the mountain alone. By the time she got home, it was already dark; she lit the lamp and sat for a long time behind the counter.
